en: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men,
and also to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory.
Janamejaya said:
"Having reached heaven, the triple-world, what realms did my ancestors— the Pāṇḍavas and the Dhārtarāṣṭras—
attain? I wish to hear this, for in my opinion, you are all-knowing."
I am not yet satiated by hearing the great deeds of all these [sages].
Having been granted permission by the great seer Vyāsa of wondrous deeds,
you indeed know everything— past, present, and future— in its true essence.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having reached heaven, the triple-world, hear what your ancestors, headed by Yudhiṣṭhira, did once they arrived there.
Having reached heaven, the third celestial realm, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma,
beheld Duryodhana seated upon his throne, endowed with splendor,
shining like the sun and encompassed by heroic glory.
Accompanied by the radiant gods and the Sādhyas of meritorious deeds,
Yudhiṣṭhira, seeing Duryodhana and beholding the splendor upon Suyodhana, was filled with indignation and suddenly turned back.
Speaking those words aloud, he said to them: "Indeed, I do not desire the worlds together with Duryodhana— that greedy man of short-sighted vision—
on whose account all this earth, as well as our friends and kinsmen, have come to such a state."
We previously defeated you by force in battle while we were suffering in the great forest;
and Draupadī, the princess of Pañcāla who walks the path of dharma, our blameless wife, was tormented in the midst of the assembly in the presence of our elders.
"May there be well-being! O gods, I have no desire to look upon Suyodhana.
I wish to go to that place where those brothers of mine are.
To him, Nārada replied as if laughing, "Do not say so!"
"O Indra among kings, residence in heaven is attained and even what is adverse perishes. O mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, do not speak thus in any way;
listen to these words of mine regarding King Duryodhana."
This King Duryodhana is honored by the thirty gods,
as well as by the virtuous and the foremost of kings who dwell here in heaven;
he has attained the destination of the world of heroes, having offered his own body as a libation in battle.
"You all, who are like gods, were encountered by him in battle;
it is he who, by virtue of the duty of a Kṣatriya, has attained this station—
he who, though facing great danger, remained undaunted as the lord of the earth."
"O son, you should not take to heart that which was caused by the gambling;
nor should you dwell upon the suffering of Draupadī,
nor on any other sufferings of yours that were brought about by the dice-game."
Whether in battles or elsewhere, you ought not to remember those things. Approach King Duryodhana according to what is right;
this is heaven, O lord of men, and here there are no enmities.
Thus addressed by Nārada, the wise Yudhiṣṭhira, king of the Kurus,
questioned his brothers and spoke these words:
"If these eternal worlds of heroes belong to Duryodhana..."
For the sake of that ignorant of dharma, that sinner, that betrayer of the earth’s friends—
on account of whom the earth was destroyed along with its horses, chariots, and elephants,
and we ourselves were consumed by grief, desiring to avenge that enmity.
Those heroic brothers of mine, great-souled and observers of mighty vows, who were true to their promises, heroes of the world, and speakers of truth—
what worlds do they now inhabit? I wish to see them.
The high-souled Karṇa, the son of Kuntī who is true to his vow, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Sātyaki, the sons of Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
and those kings who met their death by weapons in accordance with the duty of the Kṣatriyas— [all these have been slain].
"O Brahmin Nārada, where indeed are those kings? I do not see them here, O Brahmin. Have you ever seen Virāṭa, Drupada, and those others headed by Dhṛṣṭaketu anywhere in this world of heaven?"
"I wish to see Śikhaṇḍin the Pāñcālya, all the sons of Draupadī, and the invincible Abhimanyu, O Nārada.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O gods, I do not see here the son of Rādhā, who possesses immeasurable splendor,
nor the two high-souled brothers, Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas—
those great car-warriors who offered their bodies as oblations into the fire of battle."
"Where are those kings and princes who were slain for my sake in battle?
Where are all those great car-warriors whose prowess was equal to that of tigers?
Has this world also been conquered by those best of men?"
"O gods, if all those great car-warriors have reached these worlds,
know that I stand here together with those high-souled ones.
Has this imperishable and auspicious world not been attained by those kings?"
"I shall not dwell without them— those kinsmen and brothers. Indeed,
having heard my mother’s words at that time regarding the water-rites, saying,
"Let the water-offering be made for Karṇa," I am truly tormented by that.
O gods, this is what causes me to burn with grief again and again:
that upon merely seeing the feet of my mother— which were like those of that one of immeasurable power— I did not follow Karna, the crusher of enemy forces.
"Even Śakra himself could not defeat us when we are joined by Karṇa in battle.
I wish to see that son of the Sun wherever he may be,
for he was slain by Savyasācin while remaining unknown to me."
I wish to see Bhīma, of terrible prowess, who is dearer to me than my own life;
and Arjuna, who resembles Indra; and those two twins, who are like Yama himself;
and that Pāñcālī, who walks the path of righteousness.
"I do not wish to remain here; I tell you this as the truth:
O best of gods, what use have I for heaven when deprived of my brothers?
Where they are, that is my heaven; this is not considered heaven by me."
Then the gods, together with the hosts of sages, said "So be it" to his words.
The gods said:
"If you indeed have faith in that matter, O son, let us go without delay."
"For we abide by what is dear to you, by the command of the King of the Gods.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus to him, the gods then gave instructions to the divine messenger.
"O scorcher of enemies, show Yudhiṣṭhira’s friends.
Then the king, the son of Kuntī, and the messenger of the gods went together,
O tiger among kings, to where those bulls among men were.
The divine messenger went in front, while the king followed behind along a path that was inauspicious,
difficult to traverse, and frequented by those of evil deeds— a terrible road shrouded in darkness, with hair for its moss and grass.
It was filled with the stench of evildoers, a mire of flesh and blood; it was swarming with gadflies, crickets, flies,
and mosquitoes, and was surrounded on all sides by corpses scattered here and there.
It was strewn with bones and hair, teeming with worms and insects,
and surrounded on all sides by a blazing fire;
it was also assailed by crows and vultures with iron beaks.
It was filled with needle-mouthed *preta*s as large as the Vindhya mountains,
covered here and there with corpses whose arms, thighs, and hands were severed, and whose bellies and feet were cut open, all smeared with fat and blood.
The righteous king proceeded through the midst of that foul-smelling, inauspicious, and hair-raising corpse-pile, reflecting deeply;
he also beheld a river that was extremely difficult to cross and filled with hot water.
He beheld the Vaitaraṇī river, so difficult to cross, filled with pus;
and also the Forest of Sword-leaves, covered with sharpened razors;
and the heated sands of burning gravel, along with various iron rocks.
He saw iron cauldrons filled with boiling oil on all sides,
as well as the Kūṭaśālmalika tree, which is difficult to touch and covered in sharp thorns;
and the son of Kuntī beheld these tortures of those who have committed evil deeds.
Perceiving that foul odor, he spoke to the divine messenger:
"How much further must we travel on such a path as this?
And where are those brothers of mine? You ought to tell me that."
"What region is this of the gods? This I wish to know.
Having heard the speech of the King of Dharma, the messenger of the gods turned back and said to him, "Your journey has gone thus far."
"I must indeed turn back, for I was told so by the dwellers of heaven:
'O Indra among kings, if you are weary, you ought to return.
But Yudhiṣṭhira, despondent and faint from that odor,"
With his mind resolved upon returning, O Bhārata, he turned back. Having turned back, that righteous-souled one, filled with pain and grief,
heard the piteous words of those speaking all around him.
"O Dharmaja, O royal sage, O Pāṇḍava of holy lineage!
For the sake of showing us favor, stay for just a moment.
As you stand there invincible, a holy breeze begins to blow."
"O dear one, that wind which follows your fragrance has come to us with comfort;
O Lord, it refreshes us who are tormented by the heat, O Father.
Thus, O Pārtha, O bull among men, after a long time..."
"O best of kings, having seen you, we shall attain happiness. Stay for even a moment, O mighty-armed Bhārata;
while you remain, O Kauravya, this torment does not afflict us."
In that place, O King, he heard from all sides such various piteous words spoken by those in pain;
hearing those words of theirs as they spoke so wretchedly, he was moved with compassion.
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma and the best among speakers, said:
"Alas, what misery! and Yudhiṣṭhira stood there;
he indeed heard those words again and again, which he had previously heard from others.
The Pāṇḍava did not recognize those who were sick and suffering;
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, being unaware of their words, said:
"Who indeed are you, and for what purpose do you stand here?"
Thus addressed, they all then spoke out from every side, O Lord:
"I am Karṇa! I am Bhīmasena! I am Arjuna!
and also, "I am Nakula! I am Sahadeva! I am Dhṛṣṭadyumna!"
"Draupadī! The sons of Draupadī!"—thus they cried out.
O King, having heard those words at that time, which were characteristic of that region, the king then reflected: "What indeed is this that has been brought about by fate?"
What foul deed could have been committed by these high-souled ones—
by Karṇa, the sons of Draupadī, or the slender-waisted princess of Pañcāla—
that Karṇa, the sons of Draupadī, and the slender-waisted Pāñcālī [should now be here]?
"Those who are in this most dreadful place, filled with the stench of sin—
I do not know the misdeeds of all these men of meritorious deeds. Having done what, has King Suyodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, [come to this state]?"
Thus endowed with splendor, that sinful one, together with all his followers,
dwells highly honored like the majestic Mahendra.
Whose transformation is this, that these [others] have gone to hell?

They were heroes who knew all dharmas, devoted to truth and the sacred scriptures, intent on the duty of the Kṣatriyas, wise, performers of sacrifices, and givers of abundant sacrificial fees. Am I asleep or am I awake? Though conscious, I do not perceive.
"Alas, this must be a transformation of my mind, or perhaps a delusion of my intellect.
Thus King Yudhiṣṭhira reflected in many ways,
overwhelmed by pain and grief, his senses agitated by anxiety.
King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, summoned a fierce anger; he censured both the gods and Dharma itself. Tormented by that pungent odor, he spoke to the messenger of the gods.
"Go, my good man, to the presence of those for whom you are a messenger.
Indeed, let it be reported that I shall not go there, but remain where I am. For these brothers of mine, O messenger, are happy because of their reliance upon me."
Thus addressed then by the wise son of Pāṇḍu, that messenger went to where the king of the gods, Śatakratu, was staying,
and he reported what the King of Dharma intended to do.
"O lord of men, everything was exactly as spoken by the son of Dharma.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"When Pārtha had stood for a moment before Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma..."
18,003.001c O descendant of Kuru, the gods, led by Śakra, arrived there; 18,003.002a Dharma himself, embodied in form, came to behold the king,
18,003.002c arriving at that place where Yudhiṣṭhira, the king of the Kurus, was.
O King, when those gods with radiant bodies— born of merit through their past actions— had assembled there, that darkness vanished;
and the torments of the evildoers were no longer seen there.
The river Vaitaraṇī, along with the Kūṭaśālmalī tree,
the iron cauldrons, and the terrifying rocks were no longer seen;
nor were the deformed bodies that had been there on all sides.
The son of Kuntī, the king, beheld them, and they became invisible. Then, O Bhārata, a pleasant-to-the-touch, auspicious wind blew near the gods, carrying holy fragrances and being exceedingly cool.
The Maruts together with Śakra, the Vasus along with the two Aśvins, the Sādhyas, the Rudras, the Ādityas, and whatever other inhabitants of heaven there may be— all of them,
as well as the Siddhas and the supreme ṛṣis, assembled there.
Where the king of great splendor, the son of Dharma, was stationed,
there Śakra, the lord of the gods, endowed with supreme glory,
spoke these words to Yudhiṣṭhira in a consoling manner.

"O mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, the hosts of gods are pleased with you. Come, come, O tiger among men; enough has been done by this much, O Lord. Success has been attained by you, O King, and imperishable worlds are yours."
The path of brothers and friends is eternally well-honored. You must not harbor anger; listen to these words of mine:
O dear one, hell must inevitably be seen by all kings.
O bull among men, there are two heaps: that of the auspicious and that of the inauspicious.
He who first experiences the fruit of his good deeds subsequently goes to hell;
whereas he whose lot is hellish first shall afterwards attain heaven.
He who has performed mostly evil deeds first enjoys heaven;
he who has performed mostly auspicious deeds first experiences hell.
But you, O Acyuta, have performed mostly auspicious deeds, while your crookedness is slight.
Therefore, O King, desiring your welfare, I have sent you here in this manner. For you treated Droṇa with deceit regarding his son;
therefore, O King, Naraka has been shown to you by means of that very same deceit.
"Just as you are, so too are Bhīma, Pārtha, and the twins;
and likewise Kṛṣṇā Draupadī has gone to hell through a deception. Come, O tiger among men, for they have been released from their sin."
"O bull among men, behold those kings who were on your own side and were slain in battle; they have all attained heaven.
And so too has Karṇa, the great archer, the best among all wielders of weapons."
He has attained the supreme perfection for whose sake you were grieving.
O Lord, behold that tiger among men, the son of the Sun, established in his own place; O mighty-armed bull among men, cast off your sorrow.
"Behold your brothers and likewise the other kings of your own faction, each having returned to his respective place; let the fever of your mind depart.
Having previously experienced hardship, O Kaurava, from this point forward [you shall find ease]."
"18,003.020c Dwell together with me, free from sorrow and free from disease.
18,003.021a O dear one, O mighty-armed Pāṇḍava, obtain for yourself the fruit of meritorious deeds, of austerities you have mastered, and of gifts."
Today, O auspicious one, let the gods, Gandharvas, and divine Apsarases,
clothed in stainless garments, attend upon you in heaven;
[go] to the worlds won by the Rājasūya and further increased by the Aśvamedha.
"O mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, obtain the great fruit of your asceticism;
for your worlds shall be higher than those of other kings,
O Pārtha, where you will dwell like Hariścandra."
"Where the royal sage Māndhātṛ dwelt, where King Bhagīratha dwelt,
and where Bharata, the son of Duḥṣanta, dwelt— there you shall sport.
This is the holy river of the gods, O Pārtha, which purifies the three worlds."
"O Indra among kings, having bathed there in the Ākāśagaṅgā, you shall depart. By bathing here, your human nature will vanish;
you will become free from sorrow, free from exertion, and released from all enmity."
While the Lord of the Gods was speaking thus to Yudhiṣṭhira, the lord of the Kauravas,
Dharma himself, manifest in bodily form, spoke to his own son:
"O King, O highly wise one, I am pleased with you, my son."

"O King, through devotion to me, truthful speech, forgiveness, and self-restraint— this was the third test of you performed by me. You cannot be moved from your true nature, O Pārtha, by any arguments."
For previously you were tested at Dvaitavana, O Bhārata, regarding the sake of the fire-drills along with Draupadī while your brothers had perished; and you have passed through that trial.
"O son, assuming his own true form, you have been tested by me once again.
This is the third time you have desired to remain for the sake of your brothers. You are pure, O highly fortunate one; may you be happy and free from all stain."
"O Pārtha, lord of the people, your brothers are not actually staying in hell.
This is an illusion employed by Mahendra, the king of the gods.
O dear one, hell must necessarily be seen by all kings."
Therefore, you have experienced this supreme suffering for a moment;
neither Savyasācin, nor Bhīma, nor the two Yamas— those bulls among men—
nor the truthful and heroic Karṇa, O King, deserve hell for long.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, the princess Kṛṣṇā is not deserving of hell.
Come, come, O best of the Bharatas; behold the Gaṅgā, which flows through the three worlds.
Thus addressed, that royal seer, your own great-grandfather, [approached].
Service to the great guru, as well as listening to the Vedānta;
and when the Śivaliṅga in one’s own home is worshipped by the best among the knowers of Brahman— among those born of my lineage, there is no thought of superiority over Śiva.
If you have the thought that there is something superior to this [teaching] of mine, which originated from Svāyambhuva and others,
then that is merely a delusion of men.
"By your grace, let this not happen to any of those born of my lineage.
Having spoken thus with great respect regarding dharma, he addressed a certain man of noble stature,
O lord of men, as if referring to one such as yourself.
Accompanied by Dharma and all the inhabitants of the celestial realm, he went to the holy Gaṅgā, the divine river praised by the seers; having plunged into her,
the king cast off his human body.

Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, having assumed a divine form, free from enmity and devoid of all anguish, immersed himself in those waters. Thereupon, the Kuru king Yudhiṣṭhira departed, surrounded by the gods.
Accompanied by Dharma, the wise one was being praised by the great seers,
where those tigers among men— the heroic Pāṇḍavas and Dhārtarāṣṭras, freed from all anger— each attained their own respective stations.
18,004.001 Vaiśampāyana said: Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, being honored by the gods together with the Ṛṣis and the hosts of Maruts, proceeded to that place where those bulls of the Kuru race were.
There he beheld Govinda, endowed with a Brahmanic form,
indicated by a resemblance to that very same form seen before,
blazing with his own body and attended by divine weapons.

The son of Kuntī beheld Madhusūdana in his true form, being worshipped by the heroic Phalguna of great splendor, as well as by the terrible and divine beings beginning with Cakra, who possessed human forms.
Beholding both those tigers among men, Yudhiṣṭhira—
who was himself honored by the gods— received them with due honor;
and the righteous king, the enhancer of the Kuru lineage’s glory, looked upon them.
Then, in another region, the joy of the Kurus beheld Karṇa, the best among weapon-wielders, accompanied by the twelve Ādityas;
and in yet another region, he saw the Lord surrounded by the hosts of Maruts.
Then he beheld Bhīmasena endowed with that very same form—
possessing a divine body by the side of Vāyu,
endowed with supreme splendor and having attained the highest perfection.
In the place of the Aśvins, the joy of the Kurus beheld Nakula and Sahadeva, blazing with their own splendor; likewise,
he saw the princess of Pañcāla, adorned with garlands of lotuses and lilies.
Endowed with a celestial form and adorned with divine ornaments, she stood there, possessing the splendor of the sun and pervading heaven with her beauty.
Seeing her, the Lord of Śacī spoke to Dharmarāja:
"Behold her standing there, having ascended to heaven with her own body and shining with the radiance of the sun."
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira suddenly desired to question her;
thereupon the blessed Indra, the king of the gods, spoke to him.
Then the blessed Purandara indeed related [the matter] to him.

This is Śrī herself in the form of Draupadī, who has descended to the human world for your sake; she was not born from a womb, O Yudhiṣṭhira, and is beloved by the world, possessing a holy fragrance. Born in the lineage of Drupada, she has been supported by you all.
"Indeed, this [daughter] was created by the wielder of the trident for your pleasure.
O King, these five illustrious Gandharvas, radiant as fire and possessed of immeasurable power, are the sons of Draupadī and yourselves."
Behold the wise Gandharva king Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
know him to be your father’s eldest brother. This is your elder brother, O son of Kuntī, possessing the brilliance of fire.
The son of the Sun, the eldest and most excellent, renowned as Rādheya, travels accompanied by Āditya; behold him, O bull among men!
He belongs also to the Sādhyas, the gods, the Vasus, and the Maruts.
O Indra among kings, behold in these hosts the great car-warriors of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas—
heroes headed by Sātyaki and the great car-warriors of the Bhojas—
and behold the unconquered son of Subhadrā together with Soma.
[He spoke of] Abhimanyu, the great archer, whose splendor was like that of the moon.
"This great archer Pāṇḍu, united with Kuntī and Mādrī,
your father, always approaches me in his celestial chariot."
Behold King Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, accompanied by the Vasus;
observe this preceptor Droṇa at the side of Bṛhaspati.
These and other rulers of the earth, as well as your warriors, O Pāṇḍava, [are present].
Accompanied by Gandharvas, as well as Yakṣas and Puṇyajanas, they depart;
some of those best of men have even attained the state of Guhyakas,
having conquered heaven after casting off the body through their meritorious speech, intellect, and actions.
Janamejaya said:
"The high-souled Bhīṣma and Droṇa, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, both Virāṭa and Drupada, as well as Śaṅkha and Uttara— "
Dhṛṣṭaketu, Jayatsena, and King Satyajit himself; the sons of Duryodhana, and Śakuni the son of Subala;
the valiant sons of Karṇa, and King Jayadratha as well.
And Ghaṭotkaca and others, as well as those others who have not been mentioned;
and those other kings of radiant form who were mentioned there—
tell me also how long they remained in heaven.
"O best of the twice-born, does an eternal station belong to them there? Or, at the conclusion of their karma, what destination did those bulls among men attain?
O twice-born one, I wish to hear this as it is being told by you."
"For by means of your blazing asceticism, you perceive everything.
Sūta said:
"Thus addressed, that brahmin-sage was granted permission by the high-souled one."
Vyāsa began to relate this to that king.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O lord of men, everyone must go [to their end] at the conclusion of their karmas."
"Is this Prakṛti being correctly employed by you?
Listen, O King, bull of the Bharatas, to this secret of the gods,
which was spoken by the one of great splendor, divine vision, and prowess."
O descendant of Kuru, the ancient sage, the son of Parāśara, who is of great vows,
possessed of unfathomable intellect, omniscient, and the knower of the destination of all actions—
by him it was said that at the conclusion of their karma, beings enter their own bodies.
The immensely energetic and highly resplendent Bhīṣma attained the Vasus themselves;
for, O bull of the Bharatas, only eight Vasus were seen there.
Then Droṇa entered Bṛhaspati, the best of the Aṅgirases.
Kṛtavarman, the son of Hṛdika, entered the host of the Maruts;
Pradyumna entered Sanatkumāra, returning as he had come;
and Dhṛtarāṣṭra attained the difficult-to-attain worlds of the Lord of Wealth.
Accompanied by Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the illustrious Gāndhārī,
Pāṇḍu went to the abode of Mahendra together with his two wives;
as did both Virāṭa and Drupada, and King Dhṛṣṭaketu.
Niśaṭha, Akrūra, Sāmba, Bhānu, Kampa, Viḍūratha,
Bhūriśravas, Śala, and King Bhūri,
as well as Ugrasena, Kaṃsa, and the heroic Vasudeva.
And Uttara, that bull among men, together with his brother Śaṅkha—
those best of men entered into the Viśvedevas. Furthermore,
there was the son of Soma named Varcas, possessed of great luster and prowess.
That Abhimanyu became the son of Phalguna, that lion among men.
Having fought according to the duty of a Kshatriya as no other man anywhere has done,
that righteous-souled great car-warrior entered the moon at the conclusion of his life's work.
Karna entered his father Ravi, O bull among men; Śakuni attained Dvāpara, while Dhṛṣṭadyumna entered the Fire-god.
All the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra became Yātudhānas, fierce in their power.
Possessing supernatural powers and great souls, purified by weapons, they have gone to heaven. Vidura entered into Dharma alone, as did King Yudhiṣṭhira;
and the blessed Lord Ananta entered the subterranean realm.
Rāma is Śeṣa, the serpent;
that Nāga too is of great splendor,
for by the command of the Grandfather, he supported the earth through his yogic power.
He who is named Nārāyaṇa, the eternal God of gods—
Vāsudeva, who is a portion of him, entered [the body] at the conclusion of his karmic activity.
Vāsudeva, the Teacher of the World, did so for the sake of favoring the world.

Having ascended to heaven with a divine body, he remained there invisible. O Janamejaya, in the course of time, the sixteen thousand women who were the wives of Vāsudeva drowned themselves in the Sarasvatī.
Having abandoned their bodies there, they ascended once more to heaven;
having become Apsarases, they approached Vāsudeva.
As for those heroes who were great chariot-warriors slain in that great battle, [they too attained that state].
Ghaṭotkaca and all the others took refuge with the gods and the yakṣas;
those who were the companions of Duryodhana are proclaimed to have been rākṣasas,
O King, and they attained, in due course, all the unsurpassed worlds.
They entered into the Dānavas, Guhyakas, and Gandharvas; Śiśupāla became that Rāvaṇa,
and he who was the Dānava named Nikumbha, arrogant in his strength, [became Śālva].
Sṛgāla was Vāsudeva, who was struck down by Vāsudeva;
that Jarāsaṃdha was the Blessed One, who was slain by Bhīmasena;
and there was Kālanemi, the great asura known as Kaṃsa.
The one of cruel deeds, intoxicated with pride, was slain by Vāsudeva;
likewise were the Kālakeyas, the Jaṅghas,
and those hosts of Saṃśaptakas, as well as that army of Nārāyaṇa and the kings who were of great strength.
The Kaliṅgas, the Pārvatīyas, and the Kāḷīkeyas are proclaimed [to have been born from her].
Know that Draupadī was Lakṣmī, and Gāndhārī was Diti in form;
and know, O King, that Devakī, the beloved queen, was Aditi.
A great conflict arose between the gods and the Dānavas. O highly fortunate one, having conquered the mortal world, they then went to heaven,
as well as to the abode of Mahendra and that of the wise Kubera.
Those bulls among men likewise entered the worlds of Varuṇa.
O you of great splendor, O Bhārata, I have thus related to you in full detail this entire account of the deeds of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas.
18,005.026 Sūta said: Having heard this from the best of the twice-born, King Janamejaya then became exceedingly amazed during the intervals between the sacrificial rites.
Then the officiating priests brought that ritual to completion;
and Āstīka was gratified, having liberated the serpents.
Thereafter, he satisfied all those twice-born ones with sacrificial fees.
Having been honored by the king, they departed as they had come.
After dismissing those brahmins, King Janamejaya also attained supreme peace through the grace of Vyāsa’s disciple.
Then he returned from Takṣaśilā once more to the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura).
All this has been related to you as proclaimed by Vaiśampāyana;
it was narrated at the king's snake sacrifice by the command of Vyāsa.
O Brahmin, this work called an *itihāsa* is meritorious, sacred, and supreme; it was composed by the sage Kṛṣṇa, who is self-restrained, truthful,
omniscient, conversant with the ordinances, and possessed of knowledge of dharma and virtuous conduct.
By one who is beyond the senses, pure, whose self is refined through austerity,
who abides in sovereignty, who likewise knows Sāṃkhya and Yoga,
and who has awakened to many systems, having seen with the divine eye—
By him who spreads abroad the fame of the high-souled Pāṇḍavas in the world,
as well as that of other Kṣatriyas possessed of abundant wealth and splendor,
and the divine play of Vāsudeva, the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.

Having seen with divine vision, the supreme merit has been proclaimed regarding the birth and union (sāyujya) with all the portions of the Viśvedevas. The wise man who should always cause this to be heard on every sacred festival day (parvan), [attains that merit].
Having shaken off all evil and conquered heaven, he goes to the state of Brahman.
Whoever listens with a concentrated mind to this entire Veda of Kṛṣṇa,
the sin committed through the killing of a Brahmin perishes at that very moment.
Whoever causes even a single foot of this [text] to be heard by Brahmins during a *śrāddha* ceremony,
for him inexhaustible food and drink attend upon his ancestors. Having heard this sacred history (*itihāsa*), one enjoys its meritorious fruit.
This should be heard by a woman who is childless, as well as by a pregnant woman;
she shall give birth to a heroic son or a daughter destined for royal fortune.
Having heard this history, no further doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Whatever sin one commits during the day by means of the senses or even with the mind,
one is released from it after reciting the *Mahābhārata* at the evening twilight. Furthermore,
whatever evil a Brahmin commits at night while acting through his senses, [he is likewise freed from it].

By reciting the *Mahābhārata*, one is liberated from the sins of the morning twilight; the great birth of the Bharatas is called the *Mahābhārata*. He who knows its etymological derivation is liberated from all evils.
The eighteen Purāṇas and all the Dharmaśāstras, the Vedas together with their auxiliary limbs (Aṅgas), and the Mahābhārata standing on one side— let this lion’s roar of that high-souled Ṛṣi be heard.
The lordly sage Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, the author of the eighteen Purāṇas and a great ocean of the Vedas, formerly composed this entire Mahābhārata in three years.

Whatever fruit is obtained by reciting the four Vedas three times, a person who studies this [text] once attains that same fruit. Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin go to destruction for one who hears it.

She who, being virtuous, constantly listens to this [work], desiring the happiness of her lineage, gives birth to a heroic son and a daughter destined for royalty. Having heard this history, no further deliberation is required here.

By constantly listening with devotion to this great Bhārata known as the *Jaya*, O bull among the Bharatas, prosperity, fame, and knowledge shall always be attained together, pertaining to virtue, wealth, pleasure,
and liberation.
All that is accomplished here through hearing and reciting it;
what exists here exists elsewhere, and what does not exist here exists nowhere else.
Furthermore, the speaker of the *Bhārata* is a Brahman-sage and a great preceptor.
Wherein this great Bhārata, known as the *Jaya*, is constantly recited,
there Fortune, Renown, and Wisdom always abide in joy;
there is an increase of sons and grandsons, and auspicious blessings prevail.
The gods,

the Siddhas, and the supreme ṛṣis, being exceedingly delighted, worship the speaker, the listener, and the writer of the Mahābhārata; those men who do not honor the speaker of the Mahābhārata in this world [are likewise honored].
The gods would curse them, and there would be a loss of all religious rites for those men who practice [such acts]. Then,
having seated Vaiśampāyana upon a golden auspicious throne, [he spoke].
King Janamejaya and others, the twice-born headed by Āstika,
the Vaiśyas beginning with Dharmadatta, and the Śūdras such as those of the Somya lineage—
ten million, a hundred thousand, a thousand, and even a hundred.
They honored that great teacher with ten *niṣkas*.
By giving ten *niṣkas*, one whose son had died obtains immortal offspring;
and one afflicted by leprosy and other diseases becomes free from disease by giving a hundred.
By giving a thousand, those who lacked progeny obtained offspring;
they attained long life, health, sovereignty, food, and sons.
Furthermore, by the gift of ten thousand and by the gift of a million, [they attained these same rewards].

Then, when the knowledge of the identity of the individual soul and the Lord had arisen from the Great Sayings (mahāvākya), and when that which is the essence of all four Vedas had been firmly established through the worship of that very sage, his intellect became steadfast.
Gold, silver, jewels, and all kinds of ornaments;
provided with every necessary utensil and filled with hidden treasures and deposits; constructed with brick walls and free from the threat of fire and other such dangers.
On the occasion of the Svargārohaṇa festival, one should give a house equipped for the performance of deity worship, the Agnihotra sacrifice, and other recitations,
provided with both internal and external enclosures, along with a pleasure garden and cow-pens,
whether individually or collectively.
For one who desires cessation,
there is no further rebirth;
if he has desires, he shall dwell in the abode of Brahmā for a kalpa of Brahmā in happiness.
Since the knowledge of Vedānta is obtained from the mouth of the Purāṇas,
he is declared to be the Guru; indeed, worship of him is worship of the Lord.
The Siddhas and the supreme ṛṣis, filled with joy, honor the speaker, the listener, and likewise the scribe of Bhārata. Those men who do not honor the speaker of the Mahābhārata in this world—
"O gods, there would be a loss of all their ritual acts, and they would be cursed.
This history named *Jaya* should be heard by one who desires prosperity— by kings, by princes, and even by a pregnant woman."
Whatever object of desire one most cherishes, if one endowed with faith should hear this with joy, being a believer possessed of wisdom,
then the narrative of the Mahābhārata should be heard by one free from malice.
By hearing [this] even once, the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) is destroyed;
by hearing it twice with devotion, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*);
and likewise by hearing it three times with devotion, or by reciting it.
One shall attain the auspicious state of Brahman, from which there is no return. Wherever this narrative of the Mahābhārata is honored in a home, O wise ones, the god Nārāyaṇa himself dwells there.
Vāsudeva, whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals, dwells here. By remembering Vāsudeva, whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals,
the wise man who desires heaven shall obtain heaven, and he who desires victory shall obtain victory.

A pregnant woman shall obtain a son, or a daughter who will be highly fortunate. In three years, the lord Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana will compose this compilation of the Mahābhārata out of a desire for righteousness.
He composed another compendium (*saṃhitā*) consisting of six million verses.
Thirty thousand [verses] are established in the world of the gods;
fifteen should be known as being in the realm of the ancestors (*pitrya*), and fourteen in that of the *nāgas* and *yakṣas*.
One hundred thousand [verses] were indeed proclaimed among human beings;
Nārada recited them to the gods, Asita Devala to the ancestors,
Śuka to the Rākṣasas and Yakṣas, and Vaiśampāyana to mortals.
Śuka indeed caused the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas to hear [it];
Vaiśampāyana recited one hundred thousand [verses].
This meritorious history is of great significance and is equal to the Vedas.
He who causes the three castes to hear [this], placing the Brāhmaṇa at the forefront—
his self purified of all sins, pure, and with his mind fixed upon that—
having attained great fame in this world, he enjoys happiness and prosperity.
By the grace of Vyāsa, he goes again to the heavenly world.
Having understood all this, one becomes a knower of the meaning of all the Vedas;
such a twice-born man shall always be worthy of worship and worthy of honor.
The venerable Vyāsa is indeed Viṣṇu, the eternal Supreme Self.
O King, when the Svargārohaṇika Parvan has thus been completed,
one should honor the narrator with garments and likewise feed the Brāhmaṇas.

To the one who upholds the Dharma through these various dharmas and knowledges; to the divine Vāsudeva, who is to be praised here—homage, homage! Those best of men who hear this meritorious history (*itihāsa*), [attain the highest state].
The eternal heavenly worlds have been designated for their residence.
He who constantly writes the Mahābhārata from the beginning is omniscient, eloquent, and a partaker of heaven; of this there is no doubt.
Those who here recite with devotion this history known as the *Varada*,
which was composed by the best of sages and is highly venerable, shall be honored by all the most excellent of the gods.
Furthermore, the lords of sages do not fall from the celestial realms;
may this [recitation] always bring satisfaction to the speakers and listeners of the *Bhārata*,
and may the Blessed One grant auspiciousness again and again.
Having heard this *Bhārata*, all the great ṛṣis dwelling in Naimiṣa,
headed by Śaunaka, were then filled with joy in their hearts;
likewise, all the brahmins present there [praised] Sūta, the best of those who recite the Purāṇas.
They worshipped him intensely with words, embraces, and other gestures.
Then, having respectfully circumambulated the circle of sages, they spoke before the twice-born: "May there be well-being for cows and brahmins."
During the intervals between the sacrificial rites, having heard this *Bhārata* from the beginning, those great seers said, "Well spoken! Well spoken!
Having heard this foremost *Bhārata*, they spoke thus.
In the midst of the sacrifice, those bulls among the twice-born,
having honored that brahmin according to the prescribed rites and completed the ceremony,
departed for their respective homes with great joy.

O Śaunaka, that man, liberated from sin and having attained fame in this world, shall go to the highest perfection; of this I have no doubt. Even for one who studies but a single quarter-verse of the meritorious Bhārata, [the reward is great].
For one who has faith, all sins are purified without remainder.
In ancient times, the venerable great seer Vyāsa, having composed this compendium,
taught his son Śuka these four verses.
By whomsoever this meritorious compendium is heard with supreme faith and devotion, he taught it to his son Śuka;
[for him] there were thousands of mothers and fathers, and hundreds of sons and wives.
In the cycles of existence, thousands of occasions for joy and hundreds of occasions for fear have been experienced by some, and others will experience them;
these enter the fool day after day, but not the wise man.
With arms upraised, I cry out, yet no one listens to me.
From dharma come both wealth and pleasure; why, then, is it not practiced? Never from desire, never from fear, and never from greed [should one abandon it].
One should abandon even life for the sake of Dharma.
Dharma is eternal, while pleasure and pain are impermanent;
the living soul is eternal, but its cause is impermanent.
Whoever, having risen at dawn, recites this *Bhārata-sāvitrī*,
attains the fruit of the *Mahābhārata* and reaches the Supreme Brahman. Just as the blessed ocean and as the Himavat mountain, so [is this].
Both are known as treasures of jewels, and likewise the Bhārata is so called. A learned man who causes this Veda of Kṛṣṇa to be heard attains his purpose;
he shall also cast off the sin committed by killing an embryo—of this there is no doubt.

He who, with a well-concentrated mind, recites this narrative of the Mahābhārata, shall attain the supreme perfection; of this I have no doubt. For the pleasure of the Supreme Self, one should bestow various kinds of gifts.

Whatever desire one may have for the attainment of a particular fruit, that is what is prescribed. O Brahmins, after three years, the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, desiring dharma, composed this purifying Itihāsa which bestows liberation.
By a single step on the soil of Bhārata and by the sight of the Gaṅgā,
and by the mere remembrance of Viṣṇu, one is liberated from all sins;
[this is equal to] a thousand Aśvamedha sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeyas.
For those who perform the sacrificial sessions beginning with the *pākasaṃsthās* and the *somasaṃsthās*,
the fruit thereof becomes multiplied ten millionfold upon hearing the *Bhārata*. This is true even for one who eats at ten thousand Brahmins or one who goes to the Sarasvatī.
By reciting eighteen hundred thousand verses of the Goddess’s mantra, along with hundreds of recitations and fire-offerings (*japa-homa*),
and by reading to the end of the Veda, one gains that same merit as from hearing the *Bhārata*. By that [merit], all gifts have been given and great austerity has been practiced.
By him who has thus recited it one hundred thousand times, performed ablutions at sacred fords,
and heard the *Bhārata*— the wise man who has accomplished his purpose and possesses faith from beginning to middle to end— it is indeed as such.
By him, gifts of cows, land, and gold were constantly bestowed; likewise, hundreds of gifts of milch-cows and mountains were given,
as well as the gift of the world and the lineage of the Brahmāṇḍa.
By one who hears this supreme [work], it shall be as if they have performed [the rites] and given [the gifts].
Having heard this history (*itihāsa*) concerning victory, one should give it to a twice-born (*dvija*) who desires to hear it, with devotion and accompanied by [material] offerings.
An auspicious parasol, land, cattle, gold,
houses, garments, and auspicious Sarasvatī;
a twice-born man known through three generations and likewise pure in the three [modes of conduct].
A virtuous person, devoted to righteous conduct, should indeed listen to this *Jaya*. For, O Bhārata, he in whose body Viṣṇu dwells is truly a Bhārata;
one who is not a devotee of Viṣṇu should neither recite this nor even listen to it.
The Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas are the speech of Jayamaṅgala.
One should hear them only from a noble family and never from one of low birth;
therefore, [one should learn] from one who is devoted to virtuous conduct, born of a noble family, and possessed of great learning.

One should listen constantly to the Bhārata, which has descended from the two lineages through Parīkṣit. Poets are not capable of fully describing the excellence of this scripture, just as the other three stages of life cannot equal that of a virtuous householder.
Viṣṇu is the teacher, and he is likewise the listener and the scripture itself. Therefore, this *Jaya* (the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*), when heard, purifies even a sinner;
it [purifies] great sins, ordinary sins, and those sins that cause loss of caste.
Whatever causes of impurity and confusion exist here,
one should purify them by listening to this entire Bhārata;
for there is the attainment of all auspiciousness and the gathering of all prosperity.

For one who constantly listens to the *Bhārata*, there arises the gain of a son, the gain of friends, and likewise the gain of desire; the gain of a kingdom, the gain of cattle, and likewise great gain; and the gain of dharma as well.
For them there is always auspiciousness; for them there is no inauspiciousness.
Victorious, auspicious fire-offerings, propitiatory rites, and nourishing ceremonies—all these most excellent things indeed come to pass simply from listening to the *Bhārata*.

Those in whose heart dwells Hṛṣīkeśa and upon whose throat rests the Bhārata—those men in this world are blessed and have fulfilled their purpose; of this there is no doubt. For indeed, the Bhārata does not become dear to those who have not performed meritorious deeds.
Those in whose homes the *Bhārata* resides are not to be grieved for regarding what has been done or left undone. This history named *Jaya* should be heard by one desiring victory—
a Brahmin, a king, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra who is self-restrained.
Whatever has been given at Kurukṣetra, whatever bath has been taken repeatedly at Supuṣkara,
and whatever austerity has been performed on the Himālaya mountains during the proper seasons— all that belongs to him by whom the Bhārata has been heard here.
Likewise, he attains preeminence among kinsmen, preeminence in his lineage, and likewise preeminence among the social orders (varṇas).

Upon hearing this, a person shall obtain the auspicious attainment of Dharma. It shines throughout all the Vedas and brings delight to all living beings; because it enables the crossing over of all sins, it is called the Bhārata.
Immeasurable is the merit,
pure, sin-destroying, and auspicious,
that flows from the lips of Dvaipāyana for one who listens to the *Bhārata* as it is being recited.
What need has he for ablutions with the waters of Puṣkara,
who gives a hundred cows with horns adorned with gold to a Brahmin learned in the Vedas and well-versed in sacred knowledge?
And he who constantly listens to the meritorious narrative of the *Bhārata*—
the lotus-like speech of Pārāśarya, stainless and overflowing with the fragrance of the meaning of the *Gītā*— for both of them, the fruit is indeed equal.

May this lotus of the *Bhārata*, with its filaments of various narratives awakened by the awakening discourse of Hari, being joyfully sipped day after day by the bees that are the virtuous in the world, lead to our supreme welfare by destroying the impurities of the Kali age.
May the Blessed One, who is endowed with all virtues and free from all defects—
the supreme friend to me— be pleased for my delight;
he in whose hand are the mace and the discus, and whose vehicle is Garuḍa.
May that Viṣṇu, who holds a conch shell in his palm, be gracious to me.
The reciter of the Purāṇas should always be worshipped with devotion and great effort, [provided] with garments, ornaments, and so forth.
Salutation to that glorious Guru, by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance was opened with the probe of the collyrium of knowledge.
